title: Sepsis Kills 11 Million a Year. Handwashing and Vaccines Can Stop It
excerpt: World Sepsis Day put the spotlight on a condition behind one in five global deaths — and the simple prevention steps experts say too many people skip.
body:
• Sepsis — the body's out-of-control response to infection — caused an estimated 48.9 million cases and 11 million deaths worldwide in 2020, accounting for one in five of all global deaths.
  • Most cases begin as common, preventable infections. Survival hinges on early recognition and antibiotics within the first hour, but sepsis is frequently spotted too late.
  • PAHO says hand hygiene saves millions of lives every year, yet about 70 percent of health workers do not practice it routinely; vaccines against influenza, measles and meningitis also cut the risk.
  • Experts advise keeping wounds clean and covered, staying current on vaccinations, managing chronic conditions, and asking "could this be sepsis?" when an infection gets worse instead of better.

Sepsis kills more people each year than most cancers, yet it remains one of the least recognised medical emergencies. World Sepsis Day, observed on September 13, brought renewed calls from doctors and public health agencies to treat the condition — the body's runaway response to infection — with the urgency it deserves, and to prevent it with measures as basic as handwashing and vaccination. In 2020 alone there were 48.9 million sepsis cases globally and 11 million deaths — a fifth of all deaths worldwide that year, according to figures cited by Medical Dialogues. The Pan American Health Organization puts the yearly toll at roughly 31 million episodes and 6 million deaths, concentrated in low- and middle-income countries.

Context & Background

Sepsis is not an infection itself but what happens when the body's response to infection spirals out of control, damaging its own tissues and organs. "Sepsis is a life-threatening emergency where the body's response to an infection spirals out of control, leading to self-damage of organs and impaired function," Dr. Chinnadurai R, lead consultant in critical care at Aster RV Hospital, told the news agency IANS. Left untreated, it can lead to septic shock, multiple organ failure and death, PAHO says. Triggers are often ordinary — pneumonia, urinary tract infections, abdominal or bloodstream infections; influenza and Covid-19 can also set it off. The very young, the very old, and people with weakened immunity, cancer, diabetes, major trauma or burns face the highest risk, according to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control. India carries a disproportionate share: 11.3 million cases and 2.9 million deaths in 2020.

Impact & Analysis

Much of sepsis is preventable. Most cases begin as community-acquired infections, PAHO notes, and proper hand hygiene "saves millions of lives every year when performed at the right moments in care" — yet about 70 percent of health-care workers and half of surgical teams do not practice it routinely. The ECDC adds that community vaccination against measles, influenza and meningitis reduces the circulation of organisms that cause sepsis, while good hand hygiene also cuts antibiotic use — a double win against drug-resistant infections.

"Preventing sepsis starts with taking precautions such as practicing good hygiene, keeping wounds clean and covered, staying up-to-date on vaccinations, and seeking timely medical care for infections before they escalate."

— Dr. Aakashneel Bhattacharya, Consultant, Infectious Diseases, Paras Health Gurugram

When prevention fails, speed is everything: broad-spectrum antibiotics within the first hour, plus fluids, oxygen and source control, Dr. Chinnadurai said. But sepsis is often diagnosed too late because early signs — fever, rapid pulse, fast breathing — are not specific, the ECDC warns. Know the warning signs: shivering or feeling very cold, extreme pain, clammy skin, confusion, shortness of breath, racing heart. The CDC advises asking directly: "Could this infection be leading to sepsis?" Survivors can face lasting damage — chronic weakness, pain, fatigue and cognitive problems.

Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora, the numbers hit close to home: 2.9 million sepsis deaths in India in a single year means many families have elderly parents or relatives navigating hospitals where infection control can be uneven. Hand hygiene, wound care and current vaccinations matter as much during a visit to India as at home — and knowing the warning signs can be the difference between a routine infection and a catastrophe.

What's Next

In October 2024, PAHO's member states adopted a first-of-its-kind regional plan to cut the sepsis burden from 2025 to 2029 — covering awareness, vaccination, hospital hygiene and equitable access to care. For individuals, the prescription starts today: wash hands properly, keep cuts clean and covered, stay current on vaccines, manage chronic conditions, and act fast when an infection turns.
